slides.title: Hazards Assessment Report
slides.subtitle: Naples, Italy
textBlocks:
Big Question
How do Earth systems influence the hazards present to people living in different locations?

Team members and focus areas
Mariet Young - Priorities, mitigation & integration
Saniah Mcwilliams - Tectonics & geography
Stephanie Xiong-Cha - Earthquakes & ground response
Stacey Konde - Climate change
Aima Adnan - Volcanoes
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Photo: Mount Vesuvius behind Naples. Dan Dzurisin, USGS / Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, public domain.

slides.title: Which plates, direction of motion, and boundary type influence the region?
slides.subtitle: Central Mediterranean plate setting
textBlocks: Naples sits in a complex plate-boundary zone, not on a simple single boundary line.

Main driver: Africa/Nubia converges toward Eurasia across the Mediterranean.
Local complication: the Adriatic/Apulian microplate and the Apennine belt focus deformation near southern Italy.
Boundary style: mostly convergent, but with subduction, collision, extension, and strike-slip motion mixed together.
Earth-system result: mountain building, crustal faulting, and magma generation beneath the Campanian volcanic area.
mm/yr Africa–Eurasia relative motion across the Mediterranean
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Herman et al. (2015), USGS Open-File Report 2010–1083-Q; INGV Ambiente map on Africa–Eurasia convergence.

slides.title: Resulting topography and geography
slides.subtitle: Naples’ physical setting places people, infrastructure, and hazards close together.
textBlocks: Naples is built between a caldera, a stratovolcano, the sea, and a mountain belt.

West: Campi Flegrei caldera and Pozzuoli, partly within the urban area.
East/southeast: Mount Vesuvius and surrounding towns on volcanic deposits.
South/west: Gulf of Naples and Tyrrhenian Sea create coastal exposure.
Inland: the Apennines reflect tectonic compression and extension through time.
The same features that make Naples a major coastal city—flat lowlands, bays, fertile volcanic soils, and access to the sea—also concentrate population in hazardous terrain.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Image/source: Carlino (2021), Figure 1, NHESS 21, 3097–3112, CC BY 4.0; base map from Google Earth; population density inset from Regione Campania.

slides.title: Resulting earthquake regime
slides.subtitle: Earthquakes around Naples come from regional tectonics and local volcanic unrest.
textBlocks:
Regional crustal earthquakes: faults in the Southern Apennines can produce damaging shaking beyond the volcanic centers.
Deep and intermediate earthquakes: the Tyrrhenian–Calabrian system records a descending slab, showing the wider subduction setting.
Volcanic earthquakes: Campi Flegrei swarms are usually shallow and linked to bradyseism, fluids, and stress changes in the caldera.
Risk meaning for Naples: people may feel both regional tectonic shaking and frequent smaller volcanic quakes.
Italian Civil Protection describes bradyseism as uplift/subsidence that is commonly followed by shallow, low-magnitude earthquakes; earthquake frequency has increased since 2023.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Herman et al. (2015); IRIS Interactive Earthquake Browser Naples filter; Italian Civil Protection Department bradyseism page. Visual: EarthJay/USGS–Google Earth earthquake depth map, used as regional context.

slides.title: Resulting volcanic and hydrothermal regime
slides.subtitle: Subduction-related magmatism and crustal extension help explain Naples’ volcanic hazards.
textBlocks: Naples is surrounded by three active volcanic systems: Campi Flegrei, Vesuvius, and Ischia.

Vesuvius: a composite stratovolcano southeast of Naples; historically explosive and last erupted in 1944.
Campi Flegrei: a large caldera west of Naples with overlapping craters, domes, cinder cones, and hydrothermal activity.
Ischia: active volcanic island offshore; adds another nearby volcanic and seismic hazard source.
Hydrothermal signs: fumaroles, gas release, ground uplift/subsidence, and shallow earthquakes show that the system is active.
The plate setting creates magma and heat. The local volcanic systems turn that energy into eruption, ashfall, gas, ground-deformation, and earthquake hazards.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources/images: NASA Earth Observatory Campi Flegrei (2013); NASA Earth Observatory Vesuvius (2022); USGS/YVO Naples volcanoes article (2023); Smithsonian GVP Vesuvius photo, public domain.

slides.title: Part 1 takeaway: Earth systems create place-specific hazards
slides.subtitle: Connection to the assignment Big Question
textBlocks: How do Earth systems influence the hazards present to people living in different locations?
For Naples, the answer begins with plate tectonics.
Africa–Eurasia convergence creates a broad, complex plate boundary.
Subduction and back-arc extension help generate magma and heat.
Volcanism builds calderas, cones, geothermal areas, and fertile lowlands.
People live on a coast between active volcanoes and earthquake sources.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Synthesis based on Part 1 sources: Herman et al. (2015), USGS/YVO (2023), NASA Earth Observatory, Italian Civil Protection, Carlino (2021), and De Natale et al. (2020).

slides.title: Part II: Earthquakes and Ground Response
slides.subtitle: Earthquake history, faults, ground conditions, secondary hazards, and exposure
textBlocks:
Focus questions
What earthquake sources are most likely to affect Naples?
Which ground conditions can make shaking worse?
Where are people, buildings, and infrastructure most exposed?

Part II approach
Use IRIS / EarthScope earthquake mapping for seismicity.
Use INGV/DISS and USGS reports for fault and tectonic context.
Use ISPRA geology and Civil Protection data for ground response and exposure.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources for this section: Herman et al. (2015); IRIS/EarthScope; INGV/Osservatorio Vesuviano; Dipartimento della Protezione Civile; ISPRA geological mapping.

slides.title: Earthquake history and expected earthquake sources
slides.subtitle: Type, location, magnitude, and frequency of earthquakes that can affect Naples
textBlocks: Regional seismicity map for southern Italy. Use the IRIS/EarthScope link to re-export if needed.

Key points
Naples is affected by two earthquake types: regional tectonic earthquakes and shallow volcano-tectonic earthquakes.
The largest regional source is the Southern Apennine fault belt east / northeast of Naples; a key example is the 1980 Irpinia earthquake, about M 6.9.
Local Campi Flegrei, Ischia, and Vesuvius earthquakes are usually smaller, but they are shallow and close to dense neighborhoods.
M2–4 events are relatively common during unrest; M4–5 events occur occasionally; damaging M6–7 regional earthquakes are much rarer but higher consequence.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Herman et al. (2015), USGS Open-File Report 2010-1083-Q; IRIS/EarthScope Interactive Earthquake Browser; INGV CPTI15–DBMI15 catalogue.

slides.title: Major and local faults affecting Naples
slides.subtitle: Fault locations are shown as generalized, editable working labels for the slide deck
textBlocks: Generalized fault map; labels and callouts are PowerPoint objects and can be moved or edited.

Interpretation
Major regional faults in the Southern Apennines can generate the larger earthquakes that shake Campania from outside Naples.
Local structures around Campi Flegrei, Ischia, and Vesuvius are important because they are near people and infrastructure.
Regional faults are higher-magnitude sources; local volcanic faults are lower-magnitude but shallow and close to the city.
This is a generalized teaching map. Exact fault traces should be checked against DISS/INGV before final submission.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Herman et al. (2015); DISS Working Group / INGV Database of Individual Seismogenic Sources. Map redrawn as an editable classroom synthesis.

slides.title: Surface rock types and expected response to shaking
slides.subtitle: Local geology helps explain why shaking damage can vary from one neighborhood to another
textBlocks: Generalized surface materials; use an official ISPRA map for exact unit boundaries if required.

Expected shaking response
Volcanic tuff, ash, pumice, and pyroclastic deposits are common around Naples, Campi Flegrei, and Vesuvius.
Coastal lowlands, harbor areas, and reclaimed ground may include softer sediment and artificial fill that can amplify shaking.
Steep slopes with loose volcanic material can be more susceptible to earthquake-triggered landslides or rockfall.
More competent carbonate bedrock generally amplifies less, but steep bedrock slopes can still produce rockfall.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: ISPRA / Servizio Geologico d’Italia geological mapping for Napoli and Campania; Herman et al. (2015). Map is a generalized instructional synthesis.

slides.title: Earthquake-related hazards beyond shaking
slides.subtitle: Ground shaking, liquefaction, landslides / rockfall, seiches, and tsunamis
textBlocks: Generalized hazard zones for discussion; labels are editable PowerPoint objects.

Hazard summary
Strong shaking is a metro-wide concern, especially where soft sediments or thick volcanic deposits amplify ground motion.
Liquefaction is most likely in low-lying coastal, alluvial, and reclaimed areas around the harbor and waterfront.
Landslides and rockfall are concerns on steep slopes near crater margins, Vesuvius, Posillipo/Camaldoli, and the Sorrento Peninsula.
Tsunami or harbor seiche hazards are lower-probability but possible from offshore earthquakes, submarine landslides, or volcanic flank failure.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: INGV Osservatorio Vesuviano (2025) Urban ShakeMap; Dipartimento della Protezione Civile vulnerability and microzonation plan; INGV hazard context.

slides.title: Population exposure and likely loss concentration
slides.subtitle: Where earthquake hazards overlap with people, buildings, and critical infrastructure
textBlocks: Exposure shown schematically using major municipalities and infrastructure concentrations.

Exposure takeaways
Highest exposure occurs where dense population, older buildings, soft ground, and critical infrastructure overlap.
Naples, Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Portici, Ercolano, Torre del Greco, and Torre Annunziata are key communities for earthquake planning.
USGS notes that more than 3.5 million people live within about 30 km of the Naples volcanic-seismic system.
A severe regional earthquake affecting the metro area could plausibly produce multi-billion-euro losses and long disruption to housing, utilities, roads, and emergency access.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: USGS / Yellowstone Volcano Observatory (2023) population context; Dipartimento della Protezione Civile vulnerability plan. Cost is a first-pass classroom planning estimate, not an official loss model.

slides.title: Part III-A: Volcanoes
slides.subtitle: Tentative: Aima Adnan
textBlocks: Volcanoes: eruption history, exposure, and risk

Location and type of volcanic features around Naples.
Pictures of Vesuvius and Campi Flegrei.
Eruption history and 100-year planning outlook.
Vulnerable locations, likely hazards, population exposure, and cost.
Section organization follows the group role list on slide 1 and the assignment requirement to cover both volcanoes and climate change separately.

slides.title: Volcanoes around Naples: location and volcanic features
slides.subtitle: Naples sits between three active volcanic systems: Campi Flegrei, Vesuvius, and Ischia.
textBlocks:
Why this matters
Campi Flegrei is a broad caldera partly under western Naples and Pozzuoli Bay.
Vesuvius is a steep central volcano southeast of Naples.
Ischia is an offshore volcanic island with eruption and earthquake history.
Different volcanic forms create different hazards: pyroclastic flows, ash fall, lava, gas, hydrothermal activity, and volcano-tectonic earthquakes.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Map/source: De Natale et al. (2020); INGV (Campi Flegrei; Ischia); Smithsonian GVP (Campi Flegrei, Vesuvius, Ischia).

slides.title: Pictures of volcanic features in the region
slides.subtitle: The most visible volcanic hazard is Vesuvius, but Campi Flegrei affects the western urban area more directly.
textBlocks: ESA ISS image of Mount Vesuvius: crater and dense settlement around the slopes.
Campi Flegrei is not a single cone; it is a caldera with vents, craters, and hydrothermal areas embedded in the city.
Presentation point: city officials should not think only about Vesuvius. Naples’ highest volcanic-risk problem comes from overlapping volcanic systems and dense urban exposure.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Images/sources: ESA (2017) Vesuvius photograph; De Natale et al. (2020) Naples volcanic systems map; USGS/YVO (2023).

slides.title: Volcanic eruption history and probability outlook
slides.subtitle: The next 100 years cannot be predicted like a schedule, so emergency planning uses hazard zones, monitoring, and probability-based scenarios.
textBlocks:
~39 ka
Campanian Ignimbrite
Campi Flegrei caldera-forming

~15 ka
Neapolitan Yellow Tuff
Campi Flegrei

100-year eruption outlook
Campi Flegrei: non-zero probability; ongoing unrest means close monitoring and evacuation planning are essential.
Vesuvius: currently quiet but active; future eruption is expected eventually, timing uncertain.
Ischia: lower eruption probability than the two main systems, but volcanic earthquakes remain important.

Planning interpretation
Do not rank only by probability; rank by consequence × exposure × warning time.
Even a moderate explosive eruption could force mass evacuation and regional disruption.
Use monitored alert levels and pre-planned evacuation routes as the practical decision tool.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: INGV (Campi Flegrei; Ischia); Smithsonian GVP (Campi Flegrei, Vesuvius, Ischia); NASA Earth Observatory (2022); Bevilacqua et al. (2017); Civil Protection planning resources.

slides.title: Most vulnerable volcanic locations and likely hazards
slides.subtitle: Greatest volcanic risk follows the red/yellow emergency zones and the dense coastal corridor around Naples.
textBlocks:
Most likely volcanic hazards
Pyroclastic density currents: fastest and deadliest eruption hazard; evacuation is the main life-safety measure.
Ash / lapilli fall: roof collapse, poor air quality, transport shutdowns, water contamination, power disruption.
Volcano-tectonic earthquakes and bradyseism: cracking, structural damage, panic, and repeated disruption.
Hydrothermal explosions and gas: localized but dangerous near Solfatara/Pisciarelli and other vent areas.
Lahars/debris flows: most concerning around Vesuvius slopes and drainage channels after heavy rainfall.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Civil Protection Phlegraean Fields and Vesuvius planning maps; De Natale et al. (2020); INGV Campi Flegrei; Smithsonian GVP profiles.

slides.title: Volcanic disaster exposure: population affected and cost
slides.subtitle: The population at risk is unusually high because volcanic zones overlap with the Naples metropolitan area.
textBlocks:
Campi Flegrei red-zone residents
require precautionary evacuation

Vesuvius red-zone residents
face evacuation in eruption crisis

People within 20 km of possible vents
in the Naples volcanic area

Likely disaster costs
Direct costs: evacuation logistics, shelters, debris/ash cleanup, building damage, utility repairs, road and rail closure.
Indirect costs: lost tourism, port disruption, business interruption, school/hospital displacement, long-term relocation.
Planning estimate: a major volcanic crisis could plausibly create multi-billion-euro losses even if evacuation prevents mass fatalities.

Most affected places
Campi Flegrei: Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Quarto, Monte di Procida, western Naples neighborhoods.
Vesuvius: towns on the volcano flanks and ash-fall communities downwind.
Critical systems: port, rail/road corridors, hospitals, schools, water/power systems, tourism routes.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change

slides.title: Part III-B: Climate Change
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Climate change: heat, flooding, drought, and sea-level exposure

Climate risk is already visible through dangerous heat events in Italy.
By 2100, port and waterfront flooding become a larger planning concern.
These climate hazards affect public health, tourism, transportation, utilities, and emergency response.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Source base: https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/climate/climate-change-impacts

slides.title: Climate Change: heat risk in Naples
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Naples can get hot — heat risk is a public-health hazard
Stacey’s temperature slide is reframed for a city-council audience.
Stacey slide visual: high surface temperatures across Italy during hot conditions.

Hotter summers increase heat illness, cooling demand, power stress, and risk to elderly and low-income residents.
Urban areas like Naples can experience stronger heat stress because pavement and dense buildings store heat.
Mitigation connection: heat warnings, cooling centers, shade, trees, water access, and checks on vulnerable residents.
Stacey Presentation.pdf, slide “Naple Italy Can get hot”; heat-risk interpretation for Naples added for presentation clarity.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change

slides.title: Climate Change: heat is already happening
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Summer 2022 showed why heat planning matters
Summer 2022 a record-Breaking Heat Across Italy happened:

Causing Approximately 18,010 heat-related deaths during the summer of 2022.
Italy recorded one of the highest heat-related mortality rates in Europe (about 295 deaths per million people).
These findings highlight the need for heat action plans, cooling centers, and improved emergency preparedness in cities like Naples.

Heat action plans, cooling centers, and public alerts should be treated as hazard mitigation, not just weather advice.
Heat preparedness supports the final mitigation plan because it saves lives during events that are becoming more frequent.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Stacey Presentation.pdf heat mortality slide; Ballester et al. (2023), Nature Medicine, heat-related mortality in Europe during summer 2022.

slides.title: Climate Change: sea-level rise and flooding
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Port and waterfront flooding are key climate-change exposure points

Higher sea level can make storm surge, coastal flooding, and drainage backups more damaging.
The port, waterfront roads, tourism areas, utilities, and emergency routes are vulnerable because they sit near the Bay of Naples.
This connects climate change to economic disruption, not only environmental change.
Stacey Presentation.pdf flooding slide; NASA/IPCC sea-level projection resources and Climate Central listed in Stacey references.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change

slides.title: Climate change projections: temperature and precipitation
slides.subtitle: By 2050 and 2100, Campania is projected to get warmer, drier overall, and more prone to intense rainfall events.
textBlocks: Interpretation for Naples: heat stress, cooling demand, drought risk, and short-duration heavy rain all increase. Stacey's climate draft adds a real-world example: the 2022 heat wave across Italy shows why Naples needs heat alerts, cooling centers, and emergency preparedness.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Giugliano et al. (2022); IPCC AR6 Mediterranean Region (2022); Stacey draft citing Ballester et al. (2023).

slides.title: Climate change: sea level rise, flooding, and drought
slides.subtitle: Naples is coastal, so climate risk includes compound flooding: sea level rise + storm surge + intense rainfall + drainage limits.
textBlocks: 2100 planning range for city officials: about 1-3.6 ft (0.3-1.1 m) of sea-level rise under low-to-high emissions, plus local vertical ground motion from tectonic/volcanic processes. Main impacts: port flooding, drainage backflow, storm surge, and road/utility disruption.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: NASA Sea Level Projection Tool / IPCC AR6; Di Paola et al. (2021); PERI-CENE Naples flood-risk map using GHSL and WRI Aqueduct data; Stacey climate draft.

slides.title: Mariet Young
slides.subtitle: Part IV: Priorities, Mitigation & Integration
textBlocks: Turn the science into a city-council decision.
This section integrates tectonics, earthquake history, volcano risk, climate projections, exposure, and economics into one prioritized mitigation plan.
Rank the hazards using a transparent scoring method.
Recommend one integrated 10-year readiness and retrofit program.
Ask the council to approve funding, inspections, and public drills.
Workflow source: Naples Hazards final briefing plan, slides 14–18; scenario values are classroom planning estimates.

slides.title: Hazard-ranking method
slides.subtitle: A transparent 1–5 scoring system helps explain why these four hazards receive priority.
textBlocks: Priority score = 35% Exposure + 25% Human cost + 25% Economic disruption + 15% Urgency/probability
How many people and critical facilities are in the hazard zone?
Potential deaths, injuries, evacuation, and long-term displacement.
Port, hospitals, roads, tourism, housing, and business continuity.
Current unrest, historical recurrence, and timeline for action.
Scoring is a classroom planning tool: a score of 5 means highest relative concern for Naples, not a precise forecast.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Course risk framework; Civil Protection emergency zones; Iervolino et al. (2024); NIBS (2019).

slides.title: Top four hazards and expected consequences
slides.subtitle: The ranking prioritizes hazards that combine high exposure, severe human cost, and economic interruption.
textBlocks: Caldera unrest, uplift, shallow earthquakes; red/yellow volcanic planning zones.
500k red-zone residents; >800k ashfall-zone residents; mass evacuation if alarm.
Port, western Naples, housing, schools, roads, utilities, tourism.
Regional Apennine faults + shallow volcanic earthquakes; vulnerable older buildings.
Scenario estimate: hundreds to low thousands killed if severe; tens of thousands displaced.
Hospitals, rail/road network, historic buildings, emergency access.
Stratovolcano with historic eruptions; red zone requires preventive evacuation.
~700k people in red-zone plan; ashfall may force temporary removals in yellow zone.
Roof collapse risk, airports/port disruption, tourism loss, cleanup costs.
Warmer climate, heavy-rain extremes, sea-level rise, and drainage stress.
Heat illness, flood displacement, water stress; highest risk for elderly/low-income residents.
Waterfront, port, drainage, power demand, tourism, agriculture supply chain.

*Human-impact numbers are classroom planning ranges or official evacuation-zone populations, not official fatality forecasts. Deaths can be drastically reduced when warning, evacuation, retrofit, and public drills work.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Civil Protection Department (Phlegraean and Vesuvius emergency planning maps); Iervolino et al. (2024); NIBS (2019); Part III climate sources.

slides.title: Integration: why one plan must address several hazards
slides.subtitle: Naples’ top hazards are connected through Earth systems, urban exposure, and shared evacuation/lifeline needs.
textBlocks: Regional faults + shallow volcanic quakes create shaking, liquefaction, landslide risk.
Campi Flegrei and Vesuvius create pyroclastic flow, ash, gas, and unrest hazards.
Coastal fill, tuff, slopes, and dense basins amplify impacts and complicate evacuation.
Sea-level rise, heat, drought, and intense rainfall stress the same lifelines.
Same people, roads, hospitals, utilities, and warning systems are exposed to multiple hazards.

Takeaway for the council
Do not fund separate one-hazard plans; fund a single program that upgrades buildings, routes, alerts, shelters, drills, and critical lifelines together.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Herman et al. (2015); Civil Protection Department emergency planning maps; Iervolino et al. (2024); IPCC/NASA sea-level sources used in Part III.

slides.title: 10-year Multi-Hazard Readiness and Retrofit Program
slides.subtitle: One mitigation strategy that reduces losses across the top four hazards.
textBlocks:
Plan description
Focus first on Campi Flegrei/western Naples, schools, hospitals, evacuation routes, port access, and older buildings.
Combine seismic retrofit, ash-load roof checks, flood/drainage upgrades, alerts, shelters, route signs, and annual drills.

Implementation needs
Municipal engineering teams
INGV/Civil Protection coordination
Building inventory database
Public outreach in multiple languages

Expected effectiveness
Reduces collapse risk and displacement
Shortens evacuation time
Keeps hospitals, port access, and emergency routes functioning
Protects residents before the alarm phase
Protect evacuation routes, port access, utilities
Alerts, shelters, public drills, route signage
Planning budget: €1.2–€1.8 billion over 10 years, focused on high-exposure areas first; update after engineering survey and building inventory.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Civil Protection rapid/emergency planning maps; Iervolino et al. (2024) on retrofitting strategy; NIBS (2019) on mitigation benefit-cost analysis.

slides.title: Cost-benefit and call to action
slides.subtitle: The highest-value decision is to invest before warning time is short.
textBlocks: Planning estimate: what the investment buys

Expected risk reduction
Preventive evacuation can keep volcanic-death totals low if residents know routes and warnings are trusted.
Retrofitting the most critical buildings first can reduce collapse-related injuries and shelter demand.
Flood/drainage and backup-power work protects day-to-day services and post-disaster recovery.
Start Phase 1 hazard mapping, building inventory, and priority inspections.
Create a 10-year capital program with annual progress reporting.
Require annual evacuation/shelter drills for schools, hospitals, port, and neighborhoods.
Call for action: approve Phase 1 within the next budget cycle, before the next volcanic unrest or earthquake crisis limits choices.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Civil Protection emergency planning; Iervolino et al. (2024); National Institute of Building Sciences (2019). Budget is a classroom planning range, not an official municipal estimate.
